subtitle: Community engagement means more when participation actually shapes a decision. Leaders will learn to offer clear choices and accessible ways to contribute, then show a visible response to what people shared.
scope: For leaders and supervisors who sponsor public engagement in DSD or another DHS work area. This course develops an engagement plan; it does not replace required public notices, hearings, agency equity analysis, or formal decision procedures. Government-to-government matters go to the person or area responsible within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration). Practice cases do not establish policy or describe actual communities. Applicable agency duties remain in place.
introTranscript: Community engagement matters when people can recognize both the question they are helping answer and the effect their contribution had. A crowded meeting does not establish either. Leaders create the conditions: they make room in the decision schedule, explain what can change, provide accessible ways to contribute, and respond to what they learn. In this course you will work through a proposed service notice, recruitment decisions, meeting barriers, disagreement about a service change, and follow-through after a decision. You will practice distinguishing an announcement from a request for advice and a shared design process. You can use the job aid on one decision within your responsibility. Keep learning notes free of personal information, and use the responsible agency office when a formal requirement is involved.

lessons.title: Begin with the decision people can influence
lessons.summary: A useful invitation connects community knowledge to a real choice that has not already been settled.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an announcement, a request for advice, and joint development of options.
objectives: Distinguish an announcement, a request for advice, and joint development of options.
Write a clear statement of what participants can influence and who makes the final decision.
Identify one engagement promise that exceeds a leader’s actual authority.
takeaways: Information helps people understand a change; it is not the same as influence over that change.
The agency should explain which choices remain open before asking for participation.
Shared work does not erase the responsibilities of the authorized decision-maker.
lessons.statement: People can contribute with greater confidence when the invitation states a real choice and an honest limit.

image.caption: A prepared discussion starts with a decision question people can understand.

intro.heading: What is still open?
intro.body:
Before choosing a meeting format, identify the decision. A team may say it wants to engage people about a new service notice. That phrase hides several different possibilities. The team might have authority to change the notice’s wording, delivery methods, contact information, and sequence. It might have no authority to change the underlying eligibility rule. People need to know the difference. Asking them to redesign a rule that the team cannot change creates work for them and disappointment when their recommendations go nowhere.

Three useful distinctions are informing, seeking advice, and developing options together. Informing explains a decision or requirement. Seeking advice asks people to contribute knowledge that the person or area responsible will consider. Developing options together gives participants a role in identifying problems, proposing alternatives, and revising a draft across more than one discussion. None is automatically the correct approach for every situation. An urgent factual update can require a clear announcement. A notice with unresolved access problems can benefit from repeated review with people who use it.

The EPA’s public participation guide offers a framework for matching participation to possible influence. It is a planning reference here, not a DHS rule. In practice, leaders should describe the specific arrangement rather than relying on a label. Can participants rewrite a paragraph? Recommend which options should be tested? Help define success? Who will consider their recommendations, and when will that person respond? A statement such as “your feedback matters” leaves these questions unanswered.

Try a short decision statement: “We are revising the renewal notice. You can help change the order, wording, and ways people can get help. The eligibility rule is outside this review. The policy manager will decide on the final notice and explain how the review changed it.” That statement does not promise agreement. It promises an understandable opportunity. If the scope changes later, tell participants before continuing.

inThisLesson: Locate the unresolved choice behind an engagement request.
Compare three ways people may participate.
Explain decision authority without shutting down questions.
Rewrite an invitation that overpromises influence.
lessons.keyStatement: An engagement promise should name both the open choice and the responsible decision-maker.

flashcards.back: Providing clear information about a decision or requirement. The activity does not itself offer influence over that decision.
Asking people for knowledge or recommendations and explaining how they will be considered.
Working with participants across the development and revision of options, within clearly stated authority.
The responsibility and authorization to make a particular decision. It does not belong automatically to whoever facilitates the meeting.
A concrete description of what participants may influence, what is fixed, and what response they can expect.

accordion.heading: Questions that make the invitation honest

items.title: What can change?
items.body: List the choices that are actually available. A service notice might allow changes to plain language and delivery methods but not the statutory deadline. If the deadline creates a barrier, record that concern for the person or area responsible for the policy. Explaining a limit does not require pretending the concern is unimportant.

items.title: Who decides?
items.body: Name the role with authority over the decision and make that role available to hear the findings. A facilitator may collect input, while a policy manager considers it and a different office approves the document. Map this before inviting participants, so recommendations do not disappear between responsibilities.

items.title: What happens next?
items.body: Explain when participants will see the draft, how they can respond, and when they will hear what changed. Use an achievable commitment. If a decision date is uncertain, identify the next update instead of inventing a deadline. Revisit the commitment if the agency schedule changes.

tabs.heading: Match the request to the available choice

tabs.label: A decided requirement
tabs.body: The eligibility requirement is already established. Explain it accurately, offer help understanding the process, and receive concerns for the person or area responsible. Do not call the announcement a shared decision.

tabs.label: An open communication choice
tabs.body: The rule is fixed but the notice is not. Invite people to test wording, order, formats, and contact options. Their experience can change those practical choices.

tabs.label: An early service design
tabs.body: Several approaches remain possible. Invite participants before narrowing them to one preferred option. Explain resources and formal limits, and compare recommendations with other required evidence.

check.question: A team can revise the wording and delivery of a renewal notice but cannot change the eligibility rule. Which invitation is most accurate?
check.correct: Help us improve the notice’s wording and delivery. The policy manager will consider your recommendations and explain the changes; the eligibility rule is outside this review.
wrong: Help us decide who should qualify for services, even though eligibility has already been established.
Attend our engagement meeting; we will explain the final notice and will not take questions.
Our community partners will approve every detail of the notice, regardless of agency responsibilities.
check.feedbackCorrect: This names a genuine opportunity, a limit, and a response. It lets people decide whether their contribution fits the work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the invitation that matches actual authority. An announcement, an unrestricted promise, or an undefined meeting does not give a clear opportunity to influence the notice.

items.text: A bulletin explains a finalized change and its effective date.
A survey asks readers which part of a draft is confusing.
A small group develops two draft formats and revises them after testing.
An accessible recording explains how to request assistance.
Participants submit recommendations before a manager selects an option.
Participants and staff jointly choose the questions for testing alternative notices.

lessons.next: Next, examine whose experience the invitation reaches and whose experience it misses.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Priya sponsors a revision of a waiver renewal notice. The team has already written the message, selected a digital format, and scheduled release in three weeks. An invitation says, “Join us to shape the future of waiver eligibility.” The team can change notice wording and delivery but not eligibility. Priya wants community participation to matter without delaying an unrelated rule change.
scenario.prompt: What should Priya do before the invitation is sent?
options: Keep the broad invitation because it may attract more participants.
Revise the scope, keep meaningful notice choices open, and arrange a response from the responsible manager.
Remove community participation because the team cannot change eligibility.
responses: The wording attracts people to a decision the team cannot offer. It can undermine trust even if the meeting itself is welcoming.
This creates an honest and useful role. It protects the open notice decisions and names where concerns about eligibility will go.
A limit on one decision does not eliminate influence over another. People can still improve how the notice is understood and used.

lessons.transfer: Choose one upcoming invitation. Write the unresolved choice, the limits, and the role that will respond. What phrase in the current invitation would you change?

move.control: You can clarify the purpose and confirm who can act on recommendations before recruiting participants.
move.failure: People spend time recommending changes that the team never had authority to consider.
move.next: Before sending one invitation, confirm its decision statement with the responsible manager and a colleague unfamiliar with the project.

lessons.title: Look beyond the usual participants
lessons.summary: Recruitment should examine missing experiences rather than treating a familiar contact list as complete.
lessons.objective: Identify at least three perspectives missing from an existing participant list.
objectives: Identify at least three perspectives missing from an existing participant list.
Distinguish an organization’s perspective from an individual’s experience of a service.
Develop a recruitment approach that reduces one practical barrier without requesting unnecessary personal details.
takeaways: A reliable partner can offer valuable knowledge without speaking for every person affected.
People who never reached the service may know about barriers current users cannot describe.
Participation choices should respect people’s time, privacy, and freedom to decline.
lessons.statement: A strong contact list begins a conversation; it does not establish that every relevant experience has been heard.

image.caption: Empty seats can prompt a useful question about access and outreach rather than an assumption about interest.

intro.heading: Who encounters the decision?
intro.body:
Start with the experience, not a demographic quota. For a renewal notice, ask who receives it, who helps interpret it, who does not receive it reliably, and who leaves the process before renewal. People who use the service, people who recently lost access, people using a support person, and people who assist with applications may encounter different problems. Their accounts can reveal different parts of the same process. No participant should be expected to disclose a diagnosis or an entire personal history to justify contributing.

A familiar advisory group may be a good starting point. Its members can offer knowledge and suggest additional ways to reach people. It is still useful to ask how that group was recruited and which experiences are absent. An organization may focus on provider administration, while a person using services may focus on uncertainty about the next step. Both views can matter. Neither should silently replace the other. Staff should describe whose perspective a comment represents without assigning that person responsibility for an entire community.

Recruitment can favor those with predictable work hours, reliable internet, confidence in public speaking, and established relationships with the agency. A leader can change the conditions: offer a brief phone conversation, accept a written response, share questions in advance, or arrange a smaller discussion with clear support. These are examples of engagement design, not a promise that every method is suitable for every project. Ask people what would make participation possible, and work with the person or area responsible on access needs.

Consider both reach and freedom. An invitation from a case manager or provider may feel difficult to decline if a person depends on that relationship. State that participation or refusal will not determine service decisions, and avoid recruiting through pressure. Compensation or reimbursement, where authorized, should follow the applicable agency arrangements; do not promise a payment before confirming it. Record gaps honestly. If outreach does not reach people who use a different language, the final report should identify that limitation rather than describing a statewide consensus.

inThisLesson: Map experiences across a service process.
Review what a familiar contact list covers.
Offer more than one way to contribute.
Describe recruitment limits without blaming people who declined.
lessons.keyStatement: Recruit for relevant experience, and explain whose experience remains missing.

items.title: Who left before the current step?
items.body: Current service users cannot fully explain why someone never reached services. Ask whether an appropriate, privacy-conscious channel can reach people who encountered an application barrier. Do not obtain names from confidential records for a new purpose without the required authority. A gap in outreach is a finding to address, not a reason to improvise access to private information.

items.title: Who carries a different part of the work?
items.body: A family member may know about time spent gathering documents. A provider may know about submission errors. A person using services may know how the notice affected their choices. Invite these accounts as distinct perspectives. Give the person directly affected an opportunity to speak in their own way rather than routinely directing questions to someone else.

items.title: Who can decline freely?
items.body: Recruitment should explain the purpose, expected time, and use of input. A service relationship can create pressure even without an explicit threat. Avoid implying that cooperation affects eligibility or how staff will treat the person. Use a neutral contact when appropriate, and allow a person to decline without explaining why.

tabs.label: Current participants
tabs.body: Ask current participants which experiences are missing and which channels people trust. Treat their suggestions as leads to check, not proof that a group speaks for everyone.

tabs.label: Community organizations
tabs.body: Work with organizations to distribute a clear invitation. Explain the participation choices and avoid asking an organization to hand over personal contact lists without authorization.

tabs.label: Alternative formats
tabs.body: Offer brief conversations, written responses, or smaller meetings when suitable. A larger range of formats can help, but review whether those formats are accessible and whether staff can respond consistently.

check.question: A leader has heard from provider organizations but not from people using the service. What is the strongest next step?
check.correct: Retain the provider input and arrange accessible, voluntary ways to hear directly from people using the service, while documenting remaining gaps.
wrong: Describe the provider comments as the views of all service users.
Discard provider input because it can never contribute useful evidence.
Ask providers to supply all client records so staff can recruit quickly.
check.feedbackCorrect: This adds missing experience without dismissing useful existing knowledge or creating a new privacy problem.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The missing perspective needs a deliberate recruitment response. Substituting one group for another, rejecting useful evidence, or collecting records without authority does not resolve the gap.

items.text: A participant explains how the notice was read with an interpreter.
Every discussion is scheduled during weekday working hours.
No rural participants attended, so rural residents must be satisfied.
A former applicant describes where the process stopped.
The only response option requires a new online account.
One organization’s letter proves that everyone agrees.

lessons.next: Next, turn the invitation into a participation experience people can actually use.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Marcus prepares engagement on a provider referral process. Three established organizations respond promptly. His team proposes reporting that “community partners support the design.” A staff member notes that no person using services has reviewed it and the only meeting was at 2 p.m. Marcus has two weeks before the design review and no authority to access private case records for recruitment.
scenario.prompt: How can Marcus improve the evidence before the review?
options: Ask case staff to email private client lists to the engagement team.
Proceed with a broad support statement because the organizations are respected.
Keep the organizational input, revise the claim, and use approved channels offering several voluntary response options.
responses: Speed does not justify a new use of private records. Recruitment should follow approved channels and collect only necessary information.
The organizations’ knowledge matters, but the statement hides missing direct experience and the limits of recruitment.
This is a defensible next step. It widens participation, preserves useful input, and reports limits instead of turning silence into approval.

lessons.transfer: Review one participant list without naming individuals in your learning notes. Which experience is missing, and what approved invitation channel could reach it?

move.control: You can ask what the recruitment list covers and reserve time for additional outreach before the report is final.
move.failure: A convenient contact list becomes a claim that every affected person had a meaningful opportunity.
move.next: Add an experience-gap check to one engagement plan and arrange an approved outreach option for the most consequential missing perspective.

lessons.title: Make participation workable from invitation to response
lessons.summary: Access depends on the whole participation process, including preparation, communication, timing, and follow-up.
lessons.objective: Identify an access barrier before, during, and after an engagement session.
objectives: Identify an access barrier before, during, and after an engagement session.
Explain why an accessible meeting needs more than a single format or support.
Revise an engagement schedule to allow preparation and an alternative response path.
takeaways: People need understandable information before they can offer informed advice.
An accessible format does not by itself solve scheduling, pace, or trust barriers.
Ask about communication needs and work with the person or area responsible to meet them.
lessons.statement: Participation begins when the invitation arrives and continues until a person can understand the response.

image.caption: Clear materials and a workable discussion pace support participation before anyone speaks.

intro.heading: Review the whole journey
intro.body:
Imagine receiving an invitation that asks you to comment on a forty-page draft within two days. The meeting itself may have an accessible venue and captions, but the preparation window can still limit participation. A person may need time to read, use a communication support, arrange transportation, or discuss the question with someone they choose. Access planning should cover the invitation, preparation materials, the discussion, the way comments are recorded, and the response afterward.

Begin with a concise explanation of the decision and a few questions. Supply the relevant draft or alternatives in a usable form, and explain specialized terms. Do not turn a short summary into the only available information; participants who want more detail should know how to obtain it. Check whether the response method works without special software, a required account, or an unfamiliar device. Offer an appropriate alternative when the main method creates a barrier.

During a discussion, notice the pace. A participant using a communication device may finish a thought after other speakers have moved on. A person interpreting between languages may need the facilitator to pause. A quiet participant may prefer to write or speak in a smaller group. These possibilities are reasons to ask and adjust, not to assume needs from appearance or identity. The DOJ effective-communication guidance supports matching communication assistance to the person and the situation. Formal accommodation and access questions should follow the agency’s responsible process.

Build the plan around what staff can deliver. Name who sends materials, who arranges requested supports, and who receives comments through each channel. Test an online form using keyboard navigation and a realistic response. Read the invitation as someone who does not know the project. A meeting can offer useful contact without being the only chance to contribute. Let participants know which later comments can still affect the decision, and avoid a response deadline that expires before people receive accessible information.

Finally, review the follow-up format. A public summary that is difficult to read or an inaccessible attachment can exclude people after they have helped. Access is a continuing part of the relationship, not a box to check when the meeting begins.

inThisLesson: Check preparation time and materials.
Examine discussion pace and response choices.
Assign responsibility for access requests.
Test the response participants will receive.
lessons.keyStatement: Plan access across every step, and ask what works for the person taking part.

items.title: Before the session
items.body: Send the decision question, practical details, and contact for access requests. Explain what information is essential and what is optional. Use formats the intended participants can review, and allow a reasonable preparation window. A dense draft sent the night before turns the discussion into a memory test rather than a review of choices.

items.title: During the session
items.body: Explain how people can join the conversation without competing for airtime. Use a clear speaking order when helpful, pause for interpretation or communication supports, and read out important visual information. Check that a participant can contribute through the method they selected. Do not move their question to a support person simply because that is faster.

items.title: After the session
items.body: Offer a usable summary and a way to correct a misunderstood comment. Describe the next decision step and when additional input can still be considered. Follow through on promised access changes. If a participant could not use the original session, arrange an appropriate opportunity before presenting the meeting as complete participation.

tabs.label: Information
tabs.body: A plain summary can explain the choice, while a complete accessible draft supports detailed review. Use both when needed instead of choosing between simplicity and depth.

tabs.label: Communication
tabs.body: Ask the person about the method that works. Captions, interpretation, accessible text, pauses, and other assistance serve different purposes; one cannot automatically substitute for another.

tabs.label: Time and logistics
tabs.body: Consider advance materials, shorter sessions, breaks, and another response method. Confirm arrangements with the responsible staff rather than promising transport or payment that has not been authorized.

check.question: A public meeting has captions, but participants received a complex draft only the night before and must comment during the meeting. What should the leader recognize?
check.correct: Captioning addresses one barrier; preparation time and the response process also need revision so people can offer informed input.
wrong: Captioning proves that all participation barriers have been removed.
People who need more preparation should ask another participant to speak for them.
Complex information should be withheld so the meeting stays short.
check.feedbackCorrect: The leader reviews the complete process. Communication support is valuable, but access also involves time to understand and respond.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A single feature cannot establish that participation is workable. Keep substantive information available and improve the ways and time people have to use it.

sorting.heading: Place each improvement in the participation journey

items.text: Send an accessible draft with the specific questions a week before the session.
Pause so a participant using a communication device can complete a point.
Offer an accessible summary and a correction contact.
Explain how to request communication assistance in the invitation.
Read important information from a chart aloud.
Tell participants how late input can still affect the next draft.

lessons.next: Next, consider how to listen and make sense of different accounts without flattening them into a single opinion.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Elena hosts a discussion about an assessment information sheet. A participant, Owen, asks for questions beforehand and a written response option because the live pace is difficult. The team plans to provide captions and assumes that is enough. The draft has already been placed on the agenda for a decision five days after the meeting.
options: Provide the questions and accessible draft early, arrange the requested response path, and check that the decision schedule allows its consideration.
Keep the schedule and ask Owen’s support person to answer during the meeting.
Cancel the discussion rather than review the access arrangements.
responses: This responds to the actual barrier and protects the opportunity to influence the decision. Confirm arrangements through the appropriate access process.
A support person cannot automatically replace Owen’s own contribution. The pace and response method need attention.
The barrier calls for planning and assistance, not automatic exclusion or cancellation of the opportunity.

lessons.transfer: Map one invitation, discussion, and response. What barrier could arise at each stage, and which staff role will handle it?

move.control: You can schedule preparation, ask about communication needs, and confirm who will act on access requests.
move.failure: The meeting is called accessible because one feature was present, even though several people could not contribute.
move.next: Test the materials and response method for one engagement activity before recruitment begins, and adjust the decision schedule where necessary.

lessons.title: Hear disagreement without losing the meaning
lessons.summary: Leaders can separate different experiences, uncertainties, and trade-offs instead of treating participation as a vote.
lessons.objective: Separate an account of experience from a proposed solution and an unanswered question.
objectives: Separate an account of experience from a proposed solution and an unanswered question.
Identify a minority concern that would be lost in a majority-only summary.
Draft a response that explains how conflicting input will be considered.
takeaways: People can describe different realities without either account being invalid.
Frequency of a comment does not measure the severity of a barrier.
A leader should show how input was weighed rather than claim agreement that did not occur.
lessons.statement: Disagreement can reveal where a single design fits some people and creates barriers for others.

image.caption: Listening includes checking the meaning of a comment before turning it into a recommendation.

intro.heading: Do not turn every difference into a contest
intro.body:
Community participants may disagree because they encounter different conditions. One person wants every notice delivered online because mail is unreliable. Another wants paper because an online account requires assistance they cannot obtain. These accounts do not cancel each other out. They identify conditions that a delivery design should examine. A meeting organized around choosing the most popular method may miss an alternative that preserves more than one usable path.

Listen for three parts: what happened, what the person thinks should change, and what remains uncertain. “I missed the message when my account was locked” describes an experience. “Send everyone paper” proposes a solution. “Would an email alert have helped?” asks a question. Record these separately. It allows the team to retain the problem even if it cannot adopt the proposed solution. Check your understanding with the participant, using language that does not imply they must defend or prove every part of their story publicly.

Quantities matter when the information supports them, but a small engagement group is usually not a representative survey. A comment mentioned by one person can identify a serious access barrier. A repeated preference can identify a common convenience. The leader should weigh the decision implications of both. Do not describe the quieter concern as an outlier to be discarded before examining it. Also avoid treating a single story as proof of the experience of every person with a similar identity.

When accounts conflict, make the competing considerations visible. Who benefits from each option? Who might need another path? What do staff know, and what requires additional evidence? Participants can help refine these questions and test alternatives. The leader remains responsible for the decision process and any formal duties. If the discussion surfaces a complaint, a case-specific service determination, or another matter requiring a separate process, explain the appropriate route without using the public meeting to adjudicate it.

A careful summary can say: “Some participants preferred digital delivery. Others described barriers when an account was unavailable. We will test digital delivery with a usable backup path.” That is more informative than “the community supports digital access.” It preserves disagreement and explains a concrete response.

inThisLesson: Separate experience from suggested remedies.
Check a comment’s meaning with the speaker.
Weigh impact as well as frequency.
Record unresolved questions and routes for formal matters.
lessons.keyStatement: Keep the barrier visible even when the team cannot adopt the first proposed solution.

items.title: Clarify without cross-examining
items.body: Ask a question that helps understand the process: where did the difficulty occur, and what would have helped? Do not demand a diagnosis or unrelated history. Offer a private follow-up if the person wants help with their own situation. The purpose of the group discussion is to learn about the process, not to test someone’s credibility in public.

items.title: Preserve a less common concern
items.body: Include a consequential concern even if only one participant raised it. Explain that the group size limits conclusions about frequency. Investigate whether the concern indicates a design barrier and whether a low-cost alternative can address it. A concern can be important without being described as typical.

items.title: Describe the trade-off
items.body: If options compete for resources or have different effects, state the choice plainly. Explain the evidence and remaining uncertainty. Invite participants to correct assumptions and consider alternatives. Avoid presenting a resource limit as an unquestionable fact before checking it with the person or area responsible.

tabs.label: Experience
tabs.body: Record the process problem in the person’s terms and confirm the meaning. Use a de-identified summary for group reporting unless a specific authorized use requires otherwise.

tabs.label: Proposed change
tabs.body: Keep the suggestion alongside the problem it is meant to address. If the suggestion is not adopted, the problem still needs consideration.

tabs.label: Open question
tabs.body: Record what the team has not established and who will investigate it. A question should not become a conclusion because the report needs a clean ending.

check.question: Nine participants prefer an online notice; one describes losing access when their account locks. What is the most defensible summary?
check.correct: Preferences favored online delivery in this group, and an account-access barrier needs examination and a usable alternative; these comments do not establish population-wide agreement.
wrong: Ninety percent of all people using the service support online-only delivery.
The account problem can be omitted because most participants did not mention it.
The single account problem proves digital delivery can never work.
check.feedbackCorrect: The summary distinguishes the group’s views, the consequential barrier, and the limits of the evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Avoid converting a small group into a population estimate or treating one account as the whole story. Preserve both the preference and the access problem.

items.text: My online account was unavailable when I needed the notice.
Keep a paper option that does not require opening an online account.
Would a text reminder reach people whose email changes?
I needed three calls to understand which form came next.
Place the next step and help number at the top.
Do people receive the same assistance across counties?

lessons.next: Next, trace community input through revisions and the decision response.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jordan summarizes feedback on a digital service contact page. Most speakers liked a single online portal. One participant described a support worker controlling the login, while another said the portal was easier than a phone queue. The team wants a sentence declaring unanimous support so the launch can proceed. Jordan can request a short test of backup access methods before the next review.
scenario.prompt: Which response best preserves the value of the discussion?
options: Use “unanimous” because the majority favored the portal and the exceptions may confuse readers.
Cancel the portal because one person had a difficult experience.
Document the different accounts, test a backup path, and explain that the participants did not establish unanimous or statewide support.
responses: This changes the evidence to fit the desired conclusion and removes a relevant access concern.
The problem needs investigation and a workable response. The information does not support abandoning every digital option.
This keeps the useful preference and the barrier in view, then connects both to a decision that can still change.

lessons.transfer: Take a practice or de-identified comment and write its experience, proposed remedy, and unanswered question separately. Which part was missing from the original summary?

move.control: You can insist that the summary distinguish different views and evidence limits before it is used in a decision.
move.failure: A majority preference is reported as unanimous support, and the most serious access concern disappears.
move.next: Review one engagement summary with a colleague and identify any minority concern or uncertainty that needs an explicit response.

lessons.title: Show what changed and what did not
lessons.summary: Closing the feedback loop means returning a clear response with reasons, ownership, and a next opportunity.
lessons.objective: Trace a community concern to a draft revision or a documented reason for another response.
objectives: Trace a community concern to a draft revision or a documented reason for another response.
Write a decision response that distinguishes adopted changes, unresolved questions, and fixed requirements.
Identify when a changed project scope requires a new participation commitment.
takeaways: A thank-you message does not explain whether input affected the work.
A decision response should address the concern, not only the preferred solution.
Unresolved matters need a named next step rather than a promise that everything is being considered.
lessons.statement: Participants should be able to find their concerns in the response, even when the agency chooses another option.

image.caption: A record of concerns, revisions, and remaining questions makes follow-through visible.

intro.heading: Return a response people can use
intro.body:
An engagement activity creates a relationship beyond the meeting. Participants may spend time preparing, arranging support, and explaining an experience that was difficult. A general thank-you acknowledges that effort, but it does not establish what the team did with the information. A useful response connects the issue raised to the choice considered, the change made, or the reason a different approach was selected.

Consider a notice review in which participants asked for fewer pages. The team keeps some required content but moves the immediate action and help contact to the first page. A response can explain both: “You described difficulty finding the next step. We moved that information forward and tested it with readers. We retained the required explanation of appeal rights.” This does not treat every request as a command, and it does not dismiss the request because the entire notice could not be shortened.

Use a simple record with four entries: concern, response, responsible role, and next review. Protect personal information when preparing it for sharing. A report may summarize the process barrier without names or case details. If a concern requires confidential follow-up, use the authorized channel and report only what can appropriately be shared. Do not publish identifying quotations because they make the report feel more compelling.

Some matters remain unresolved. Label them as questions with the next action and an achievable update point. If research is needed, say what will be investigated. If another office holds the authority, describe where the concern has been sent without promising that office’s result. If a project changes substantially, revisit the invitation: a group recruited to review wording has not necessarily reviewed a new delivery model. Do not stretch its previous participation into endorsement of an expanded proposal.

The response is also a check on internal follow-through. If staff cannot explain how input affected the draft, the issue may be more than communication. Perhaps participation came too late, authority was unclear, or a revision was lost. Leaders can use the record to correct the process before repeating it.

inThisLesson: Connect concerns to the actual draft.
Explain retained requirements without dismissing input.
Protect identity in shared summaries.
Assign unresolved matters a response point.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear response describes what happened to the concern and who owns the next step.

items.title: A change was made
items.body: Describe the revision and why it addresses the concern. Be specific enough for a participant to recognize it. “We improved accessibility” is less useful than “we added a telephone response option and revised the instructions tested by readers.” Do not claim the change solved the barrier until the evidence supports that conclusion.

items.title: Another approach was chosen
items.body: Explain the concern and the alternatives considered. State why the chosen option was selected and how its effects will be reviewed. People do not need agreement on every recommendation to receive a respectful account of the decision. Avoid referring to “agency needs” without naming the actual limit or responsibility.

items.title: A question remains
items.body: Identify what is not known and what will happen next. Do not use “under consideration” as a permanent answer. A named responsible role and update point let participants know where the matter stands. If an office declines to act, record that outcome accurately rather than leaving an open task forever.

tabs.heading: What to include in the return message

tabs.label: The concern
tabs.body: Use a concise, de-identified account of the issue. Separate a person’s experience from the team’s interpretation, and offer a way to correct a misunderstanding.

tabs.label: The decision
tabs.body: State the change, retained requirement, or selected alternative. Include the reason and avoid claiming agreement from participants who expressed different views.

tabs.label: The next check
tabs.body: Describe how staff will see whether the change helped and when an update is expected. Keep commitments within confirmed authority and capacity.

check.question: Participants asked for a shorter notice. Staff retained a required rights explanation but moved the next step to the first page. Which response is strongest?
check.correct: Explain the concern, show the revised next-step placement, identify the retained rights content, and describe how the revised notice will be tested.
wrong: Say every recommendation was accepted because the first page changed.
Send a thank-you without discussing the revision or the retained content.
Say participants did not understand the law and therefore their comments were unhelpful.
check.feedbackCorrect: This response recognizes the underlying concern and explains a practical revision without concealing the limit.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The response needs to connect the concern to the actual work. Overclaiming, silence, or dismissive language does not establish follow-through.

items.text: The revised draft now puts the help number beside the deadline.
Staff do not yet know whether text reminders are feasible.
Required appeal-rights language remains in the notice.
Readers tested and improved the order of the instructions.
Another office must examine the request to change the underlying rule.
The team selected phone and paper alternatives instead of the proposed new app.

lessons.next: Next, bring the planning and follow-through steps together for one decision in your work.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Aisha’s team held two discussions about a service notice. Participants asked for a shorter notice and a phone option. Staff added the phone option but kept a required rights section. A communications draft says, “We listened and adopted your ideas.” Aisha also learns that a future version may combine the notice with a new account-registration process that participants never reviewed.
scenario.prompt: What should Aisha change before sending the response?
options: Use the positive sentence because detail may invite disagreement.
Describe the specific changes and retained content, and keep the future account process outside the claim of reviewed work.
Delay all responses until every future project decision has been made.
responses: The sentence hides the important limit and could wrongly imply that participants shaped the future account process.
This gives participants a truthful response and preserves a separate opportunity to review a materially different process.
Participants deserve an update on the work they helped with. Later decisions do not justify indefinite silence about completed changes.

lessons.transfer: Choose one engagement concern and write a four-entry response: concern, action or reason, responsible role, and next check. What can safely be shared?

move.control: You can require a decision response and confirm that its claims match the work participants actually reviewed.
move.failure: The public message says “we listened” while the revision record cannot show what changed or why.
move.next: Before closing one engagement activity, prepare an accessible response reviewed by the responsible decision-maker and provide a correction contact.

lessons.title: Build an engagement plan you can carry through
lessons.summary: A small, complete plan is more useful than a large calendar of activities disconnected from the decision.
lessons.objective: Draft an engagement plan containing a decision question, participation promise, access arrangements, response process, and review point.
objectives: Draft an engagement plan containing a decision question, participation promise, access arrangements, response process, and review point.
Select two measures of participation quality that go beyond attendance.
Identify one formal duty that must remain separate from the engagement plan.
takeaways: Plan backward from the decision while leaving genuine time to change it.
Evaluate whether people could contribute and whether their concerns affected the work.
Consultant support can strengthen the process while staff retain responsibility for their own work.
lessons.statement: The purpose of the plan is to protect a meaningful opportunity from invitation through follow-through.

image.caption: An engagement plan works when responsibility is shared clearly and the next decision remains visible.

intro.heading: A plan small enough to use
intro.body:
Select one decision with an open choice and a responsible manager. Write the question in terms people can recognize. “How can the renewal notice help people take the next step?” is more useful than “How can we optimize stakeholder engagement?” State the limits, the expected influence, and the role that will respond. Then identify which experiences the plan should reach and which approved channels can offer a voluntary invitation.

Put preparation and access on the calendar before the decision deadline. Include time to receive and revise the draft, review requested communication assistance, and consider contributions arriving through alternative channels. A meeting date is only one part of the schedule. If the decision must occur before meaningful input could be considered, change the promise: explain what can be informed now and what will be reviewed next. Do not describe a rushed announcement as a shared design process.

Choose a simple way to record concerns, changes, questions, and responsible roles. Use approved locations and privacy practices for actual project records. Private learning notes should not contain identifying service information. Decide who will review the summary for accuracy, who will make the decision, and who will return the response. These roles may involve the same person in a small project, but the responsibility should still be clear.

Evaluate the opportunity, not just the event. Attendance can describe reach, but it does not establish useful influence. Ask whether participants understood the decision, could contribute in their chosen way, saw their concerns represented accurately, and received an explanation of the result. Review whose experience remained missing. Record a change in the draft and examine whether it improved the process. A project can have many attendees and little influence; a smaller, well-supported discussion can produce an important revision without representing everyone.

Use consultant support as guidance when needed. Staff can prepare the plan, analyze what they heard, and develop their own recommendations. The consultant can help challenge assumptions and offer feedback. Neither the consultant nor this course replaces formal agency decisions, required hearings, or government-to-government processes. The finished plan should tell a colleague exactly what the next engagement step is and why it matters to the decision.

inThisLesson: Draft a practical participation plan.
Protect time for review and revision.
Choose meaningful quality checks.
Connect the plan to formal responsibilities and optional support.
lessons.keyStatement: Measure whether the opportunity worked and what it changed, not simply how many activities occurred.

items.title: Is the opportunity real?
items.body: Check that at least one meaningful choice is open, that the decision-maker agrees to consider input, and that the calendar permits changes. If any part is missing, repair it or narrow the invitation honestly. A plan cannot create authority by using more collaborative language.

items.title: Can people use it?
items.body: Check recruitment, preparation, communication, and follow-up. Assign access arrangements to a responsible role and confirm the response options are workable. Note gaps you cannot resolve before the decision, so the report does not suggest that people had opportunities they did not actually receive.

items.title: Can the team finish the response?
items.body: Reserve staff time for synthesis, revision and the return message. A meeting can create more findings than the team expected. Identify which require action, another office, or further evidence. The final record should distinguish these rather than marking every concern complete because the session ended.

tabs.heading: Useful checks for the next cycle

tabs.label: Reach
tabs.body: Which relevant experiences were heard, and which remain missing? Report the scope of the participants without treating a convenience group as a representative sample.

tabs.label: Participation
tabs.body: Could people understand the choices and contribute through a suitable method? Ask participants directly and examine access problems raised during the process.

tabs.label: Influence and response
tabs.body: Which concern changed the draft or triggered another review? Did the response explain the outcome accurately, and did staff complete promised next steps?

check.question: Which pair of measures best complements an attendance count?
check.correct: Whether participants could contribute meaningfully and whether the decision response showed what changed or why another approach was chosen.
wrong: The number of slides shown and the length of the manager’s presentation.
The percentage of comments that praised the agency and the number of social-media reactions.
The number of meetings held and whether the team declared engagement complete.
check.feedbackCorrect: These checks examine the quality and consequence of participation. Attendance can still describe reach, but it cannot answer those questions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Activity totals and positive reactions do not establish that participants had influence or received a clear response. Choose measures tied to the purpose of engagement.

items.text: Confirm the open choices, limits, and response owner.
Examine missing experiences and unresolved access barriers in the findings.
Return an accessible account of changes and remaining questions.
Check recruitment channels and preparation materials.
Compare the draft with the concerns participants raised.
Review whether promised next steps occurred.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare one engagement plan. The related course on centering people with disabilities develops the shared design role in greater depth.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Theo has a six-week window to improve instructions for arranging a service-planning meeting. Staff propose three listening sessions and a satisfaction poll. No one has named the choices participants can influence, and the final manager review is scheduled before the last session. Theo can rearrange the schedule and ask the consultant for feedback on the plan.
options: Clarify the decision and roles, move input before the manager review, provide workable access options, and reserve time for a decision response.
Hold all three sessions and report attendance as evidence that the instructions were developed with the community.
Ask the consultant to perform the engagement so the team can continue its other work.
responses: This connects the activities to actual influence and carries responsibility through the decision and response. Consultant feedback can strengthen it without replacing the team’s work.
Attendance alone cannot establish how the instructions changed, and input arriving after review has little opportunity to influence them.
Guidance can be valuable, but staff should build their capacity and retain ownership of their project work rather than transfer the whole task.

lessons.transfer: Draft a one-page plan for a decision you influence. Ask a colleague to identify the open choice, missing experiences, access arrangements, and response owner without explanation from you.

move.control: You can connect the activity calendar to the decision, assign follow-through, and request guidance while carrying out your own work.
move.failure: A sequence of meetings is completed, but participation quality and its effect on the decision remain unknown.
move.next: Within your next project-planning cycle, use the job aid to prepare one engagement plan and review it with the responsible decision-maker.

jobAid.subtitle: A one-page plan from an open decision to a clear response.
remember: State the open choice and the limits before asking for time.
Hear relevant experiences through accessible, voluntary channels.
Show what changed, what did not, and what comes next.

sections.heading: Define the opportunity
items: Write the decision question in familiar terms.
List what participants can change and what is fixed.
Name the role that decides and the role that returns the response.

sections.heading: Reach and prepare
items: Identify experiences missing from the familiar contact list.
Choose approved outreach channels without collecting unnecessary personal information.
Send understandable materials and offer suitable response choices.
Confirm requested communication support through the responsible agency process.

sections.heading: Listen and examine
items: Separate experiences, suggested changes, and unanswered questions.
Check the meaning of comments rather than inferring motives.
Retain consequential minority concerns and describe evidence limits.
Route formal complaints, service determinations and government-to-government matters to the designated people or areas.

sections.heading: Decide and respond
items: Record each significant concern and its action, reason, or next investigation.
Check that input arrived while the decision could still change.
Share a usable response without identifying private details.
Explain material changes in scope and offer another review when needed.

sections.heading: Review the opportunity
items: Ask whether people could understand and contribute.
Identify what participation changed and whether the response was completed.
Use consultant guidance to strengthen the next cycle while staff carry out their own work.
